As of 240 AM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Typical summer weather today with scattered 
thunderstorms near the coast from early afternoon through early 
evening.

Northwest upper/mid level flow continues to prevail over the 
forecast area early this morning with strong ridging over the 
central/southern CONUS and troughing over New England and offshore. 
A weak surface boundary is bisecting the area while an upper 
shortwave tracks over us at the same time. These features have been 
responsible for the storms we have seen in the Piedmont since last 
evening, with some very impressive storms in Louisa County and near 
Farmville. The kinematic environment remains strong with 40 kt of 
effective shear even though instability is modest given the loss of 
daytime heating. Expect storms to persist (mainly west of the bay) 
for the next few hours before gradually weakening as we head toward 
sunrise. 

That weak boundary settles near the coast today with NW flow aloft 
continuing. Scattered tstms are expected to initiate along sea 
breeze boundaries by early afternoon, and persist through early 
evening before dissipating by 10-11 PM. Storm timing today should be 
closer to climatological norms when compared to the very late timing 
yesterday. Storms will likely spread slightly inland during the late 
aftn/early evening, but will struggle to make it to the I-95 
Corridor. With the NW flow remaining in place, 25-30 kt of bulk 
shear, and moderate sfc-based instability, a few stronger storms are 
possible with the main threat being damaging winds, though large 
hail can't completely be ruled out. In addition to the severe 
threat, localized flooding is possible as the storms will be 
somewhat slow moving and will likely impact the urban areas of SE 
VA. The HREF ensemble has 30% probs of 3" of rain in 3 hours across 
SE VA/NE NC, with at least 10% probs for 3"/3 hours in other coastal 
areas. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Widespread showers and thunderstorms expected 
Tuesday afternoon and evening with better potential for severe 
weather. The main threat is damaging wind gusts with large hail also 
possible.

The set-up Tuesday continues to suggest that this will be the best 
shot at thunderstorms, with a decent chance for severe weather. An 
anomalously strong upper trough and sfc low are progged to deepen 
over the Northeast CONUS. In fact, the low could deepen to 993mb 
with -2 to -3 sigma height anomalies over the northern Mid-
Atlantic/Northeast. The synoptic features are impressive especially 
considering it is late July. There will be a belt of 40-50 kt 500mb 
winds on the SW side of the trough that may move over the local area 
during the aftn. At the same time, the low will drag a cold front 
toward the area. Where there is a slight chance of showers and 
storms in the morning, the main window of concern is expected to be 
from 2-10 PM. Storms likely initiate near our northern CWA border 
during the afternoon before potentially moving SE through the area 
during the evening. Storms move offshore Tuesday night as the front 
moves through and winds become NW.  Given the 500mb flow, impressive 
shear by July standards, and mid level lapse rates up to 
6.5C...there could be a robust damaging wind and hail threat. Can't 
completely rule out a brief tornado near the coast as LLVL winds 
will be more backed here. SPC has maintained the Slight Risk (Level 
2/5) for severe wx across the entire area. While the parameters look 
decent for severe wx, we will have to watch upstream 
overnight/morning MCS activity which is the main thing that could 
result in a lower severe threat than anticipated (especially across 
north and northeast portions of the FA). Highs Tuesday look to be in 
the upper 80s to around 90F, along with humid conditions with dew 
points in low-mid 70s. Storms will be moving quickly, which will act 
to limit flooding, but cannot rule out localized flash-flooding, 
mainly in urban/flood prone areas. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Isolated showers and storms are possible on 
Wednesday, with mainly dry weather to end the week. Temperatures 
drop to slightly below average late this week. 

The low pressure system at the surface and aloft is progged to 
linger over the Northeast CONUS from Wednesday-Friday. With the 
closer proximity of the upper low, there cold be some showers/storms 
on Wednesday (mainly late in the day). Thursday through Friday looks 
mostly dry, with near to slightly below average temperatures, as 
LLVL flow will continue to be out of the NW.
